title: Clothes for Israel's High Priest
overview: God tells Moses to set apart Aaron and his sons as priests and describes in detail the special clothing they are to wear when serving at the sacred tent.

parts.label: Aaron's family chosen (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: As Israel became a nation with one shared place of worship, Aaron and his four sons were set apart as its priests, and the priesthood would pass down through his family. Their clothes were called holy not because the cloth itself was special but because they were worn only for sacred duties, giving the office dignity in the people's eyes.

parts.label: The ephod and shoulder stones (vv. 6-14)
parts.note: The ephod was a richly woven sleeveless garment, something like a vest or apron, held up by shoulder straps. On each shoulder sat an onyx stone carved with six names of Israel's twelve tribes, so that Aaron literally carried the whole people before God whenever he served.

parts.label: The breastpiece over his heart (vv. 15-30)
parts.note: A square pouch of the same fabric held twelve gemstones, one for each tribe, so the people's names rested over Aaron's heart. Inside it went the Urim and Thummim, objects used somehow to seek God's decisions; no one today knows exactly what they were or how they worked, and some of the gem names are also uncertain.

parts.label: The blue robe with bells (vv. 31-35)
parts.note: Under the ephod Aaron wore a blue robe whose hem alternated cloth pomegranates and small gold bells that rang as he moved in and out of the Holy Place. The text ties the bells to his not dying, which shows how seriously coming near God was taken, though why the bells mattered is debated, perhaps as proof he came properly dressed or as a signal to the people outside.

parts.label: The gold plate on the turban (vv. 36-38)
parts.note: A gold plate engraved with words declaring him set apart for the LORD was tied to the front of his turban, marking Aaron as the one who carried the blame for any fault in the people's offerings so their gifts could still be accepted. Christians later read this, and the names he carried, as a picture of Jesus standing before God on behalf of others.

parts.label: Sons' clothes and ordination (vv. 39-43)
parts.note: Aaron's sons received simpler linen tunics, sashes and caps, and then all of them were to be anointed with oil and formally installed as priests. Linen undergarments were required so their bodies stayed covered while serving at the altar, and failing to wear them was treated as a guilt serious enough to bring death.

disagreement: Christians differ over how much of this detail should be read as symbols pointing to Christ and how much is simply a record of how ancient Israel's worship was arranged.
think: Have you ever had someone represent you or speak on your behalf, and what made that feel trustworthy or not?
